cards.front: What determines the order of elements in the periodic table, and what is atomic number?
cards.back: Elements are arranged by increasing **atomic number**, the number of protons in an atom's nucleus. Atomic number, not atomic mass, determines an element's position.

cards.front: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical properties?
cards.back: They have the same number of **outer-shell electrons**, and these electrons influence how an element reacts.
cards.hint: Think about what stays the same down a column.

cards.front: Where are most metals and most non-metals found in the periodic table?
cards.back: Most **metals** lie on the left-hand side and in the centre; most **non-metals** lie towards the right-hand side.
The **one- or two-letter abbreviation** used to represent an element. The first letter is always a capital and any second letter is lower case.

cards.front: What are the chemical symbol and atomic number of sodium?
cards.back: The symbol is $\text{Na}$ and the atomic number is $11$.
cards.hint: Find sodium's name in the table and read across its entry.

cards.front: A student writes the symbol for sodium as $\text{NA}$. What is wrong with this?
cards.back: The **second letter must be lower case**, so the correct symbol is $\text{Na}$. Only the first letter is a capital.

cards.front: What is the difference between a group and a period?
cards.back: A **group** is a vertical column whose elements have the same number of outer-shell electrons; a **period** is a horizontal row whose elements have the same number of occupied electron shells.
cards.hint: Consider which direction each one runs across the table.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say that elements in the same period have similar chemical properties?
cards.back: Similar chemical properties belong to **groups**, not periods. Across a period the outer-shell electron numbers change, so properties differ.
cards.hint: Consider which of the two patterns produces similar properties.

cards.back: Elements that generally **conduct heat and electricity well** and can often be bent into shape. Many are also shiny.
Elements that generally **conduct heat and electricity poorly**. They often have lower melting points than metals, though there are exceptions.
cards.hint: Compare with the properties of metals.

cards.front: Why is hydrogen not a metal, even though it sits above Group 1?
cards.back: Hydrogen is a **non-metal** despite its position above Group 1. Position is a useful starting point, but it is the exception here.
cards.hint: Think about where the reactive metals in Group 1 are found.

cards.front: How do Group 1 metals such as lithium and sodium react with water?
cards.back: They form a **metal hydroxide** and **hydrogen**. Group 1 contains reactive metals.

cards.front: How do Group 7 elements such as chlorine and bromine react with metals?
cards.back: They form **salts**. Group 7 contains reactive non-metals, also called halogens.
cards.hint: Consider what type of element Group 7 contains.

cards.front: Why are the Group 0 gases such as helium and neon so unreactive?
cards.back: Their **outer electron shells are full**, so they have very little tendency to react.
cards.hint: Compare with the reason elements in the same group behave alike.
